newsitem.title: VIETNAM: FEATURE - Hunting days are over for Vietnam's elephant kings.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hunting days are over for Vietnam's elephant kings.

text.p: For the price of a few dollars from camera-toting tourists, Y Prung Eban will don his garish hunting garb, slurp rice wine from an earthern jar and then ride majestically on the back of an elephant.

Times have changed for 78-year-old Eban, a member of Vietnam's Ede ethnic minority and one of the last of a legendary circle of heroic elephant trackers in the central highlands' Yok Don National Park.
"I'm eager to go out and find more," he says, brandishing a buffalo-hide hoop that used to snag wild elephants as they crashed through Yok Don's tropical jungle.
But Eban's hunting days are over.
There are just 200 to 400 wild elephants roaming the forests of Vietnam, less than 25 percent of the estimated population at the height of the Vietnam War in the 1970s.
"The odds are so heavily stacked against the elephant," says Shantini Dawson of the Britain-based conservation group, Flora and Fauna International (FFI).
"If the...population keeps going down at this rate there won't be any elephants left by the next century," she said.
The 20th Century has been a rough ride for the Asian elephant in Vietnam.

For years they were hunted for tusk, tooth, hide and meat. Beasts of burden for North Vietnam during the war, they were bombed by the Americans, and their habitats were scarred by war-time defoliants and then decimated by extensive logging.
A stack of plans to save the species from extinction gathered dust for years due to a lack of funding, coordination and political will.

Now, with the help of FFI, the government has launched a drive to save the species, a reflection of its new-found concern about neglect of the environment and nature during years of focus on economic development.

Despite global disapproval, there is still a market for elephant ivory. Villagers near the Yok Don National Park say one tusk can sell for $1,000. That is about four times the average annual income in Vietnam, one of the world's poorest countries.
But authorities no longer ignore illegal elephant hunting. Four people were jailed in the central highlands last month, one of them for 20 years, for killing an elephant for its tusks.
The new preservation project will focus on three national parks or extensive forest areas where, because of population size, the species stands its best chance of survival.
Detailed surveys will be carried out, managed reserves will be set up and special "elephant guards" -- complete with uniforms -- will be put in place to watch out for hunters.
But in Ban Don, a poor, ethnic minority village on the edge of the Yok Don park, there seems to be more interest in selling the hunting legend to tourists than in conservation.
A ride on one of the 44 domesticated elephants there will set you back $30 an hour.

Eban, between raucous blasts on an ivory hunting horn, will boast that he captured nearly 300 elephants since the age of 13 and then give an exhaustive rundown -- in a mixture of Lao, Vietnamese and halting French -- of quirky trapper traditions.
Before going out into the jungle, he says, a tracker would live apart from his wife for one month: if he touched her during that time, he would have bad luck in the hunt.
Misfortune, in the form of a fine measured in buffaloes, would also befall the hunter if he trapped his prey by a left foot rather than a right.

Eban will also show you the spire-topped stone mausoleum of Ma Krong, the "Elephant King" who was awarded a Legion d'Honneur from Vietnam's former French colonial masters for his tracking skills before he died in the 1940s.
Other celebrated hunters of a bygone era are buried nearby in tombs that, local people say, are littered with elephant bones and buffalo skulls.
Back at the national park centre, Eban heads off to change into Western-style trousers and T-shirt, and then turns up again for his tour guide fee.
